title: Few lovers of the cross (II.11)
hook: many follow Jesus to the breaking of bread, few to the cup
tomorrow: can carrying something heavy ever make it lighter?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a familiar friend: Mary rising at one word, and the great art of talking with Jesus, close enough that nobody has to knock. The line was a familiar friend.

The party's over. The music's off, cups are everywhere, and the room that held a crowd now holds three people with trash bags. Every gathering has that crew, the ones still there when the fun has left, folding the chairs. The Imitation noticed the same split in Jesus's own story. There's a long table where bread is broken and every seat is taken. Later that night, in the garden of Gethsemane, he prays that a cup might pass from him, and his friends fall asleep.
screen: `THE PARTY'S OVER.` → `THE ONES WITH TRASH BAGS.` → `A FULL TABLE, A SLEEPING GARDEN.`

segments.voice: Chapter eleven of book two lays it out in pairs. Jesus has many lovers of his heavenly kingdom, it says, but few who carry his cross. Many want comfort; few want trouble. Many will sit at his table; few will fast with him. Then the line the day is built on: many follow him as far as the breaking of bread, few as far as drinking the cup of his passion. Many admire the miracles; few follow him into the shame of the cross. The chapter isn't sneering at anyone. It's a mirror, and the reader is meant to look into it, not at the neighbor. Then the turn, and it's a hard one. Those who love Jesus for himself, the chapter says, bless him in trouble as much as in the highest joy, and even if he never gave them comfort, they would still praise him and give thanks. That's the test of love it cares about: not how you show up to the feast, but whether you stay for the garden. In an ordinary week that can look small, almost invisible. The bus ride home after a loss. A hospital waiting room. The friend who's still crying after everyone else has gone home. The table is easy to find. The cup is where friends are counted.
screen: `MANY AT THE TABLE, FEW AT THE FAST.` · `THE BREAD, THEN THE CUP.` · `A MIRROR, NOT A FINGER.` · `LOVED FOR HIMSELF.` · then, large: `FEW FOLLOW TO THE CUP.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and bring to mind one hard thing you're in the middle of: a worry, an ache, a waiting. Instead of hurrying out of it, stay beside it for the sit, breathing slowly, the way a friend keeps watch through a long night. If you pray, you can offer it as a small share of his cup.
Few lovers of the cross. The Imitation's mirror: many follow Jesus to the breaking of bread, few to the cup of his passion.
screen: `FEW LOVERS OF THE CROSS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Keep this one: to the cup, where the friends who stay get counted, quietly. Rest easy tonight.

chat.says: lost in overtime. season's over. half the team bolted, valeria's crying on the bus. i want to bolt too.

Go. Staying for the hard part is for whoever lost the game, and it wasn't only you.
Stay, but cheer her up fast. Following to the cup means fixing the sad part quickly.
chat.meaning: The Imitation says many follow Jesus to the breaking of bread, few to the cup. Staying in the hard moment is the cup.

Gethsemane.meaning: the garden where Jesus prayed the night before he died

notes: Imitation II.11 paraphrased: Jesus has many lovers of his heavenly kingdom but few bearers of his cross; many desirers of consolation, few of tribulation; many companions of his table, few of his abstinence; many follow him to the breaking of bread, few to drinking the cup of his passion; many reverence his miracles, few follow the shame of his cross; those who love Jesus for Jesus' sake bless him in tribulation as in consolation, and would praise him even if he never gave consolation. Confirm each against the Latin.
Gethsemane scene paraphrased from Matthew 26:36–45 (the cup, 'not as I will', the disciples sleeping). Not quoted.
'Many' and 'few' are the chapter's own words; no count is claimed. 'Half the team bolted' is Sofia's own exaggeration in the chat, not a lesson claim.
